title: Inference Scheduling: Protecting Latency While Keeping GPUs Busy
summary: Reason about continuous batching, competing prefill and decode work, overload control, speculation, and disaggregation using explicit latency budgets and queue arithmetic.
learningObjectives: Separate queue time, first-token latency, decode cadence, throughput, and goodput.
Design a continuous scheduler with compute and KV-memory admission constraints.
Explain chunked prefill, speculative decoding correctness, and when phase disaggregation helps.
Defend a latency policy using a worked example and a reproducible load-test plan.

sections.title: 1. Start with the service contract
paragraphs: An inference scheduler chooses which request tokens run next on shared hardware. Its objective is rarely maximum tokens per second alone. A chat product may need a prompt response and smooth streaming; offline summarization may tolerate minutes of waiting. Define the workload before choosing a policy: arrival bursts, prompt-length distribution, requested output limits, tenant weights, and the fraction of requests that cancel. These are inputs to the design, not incidental benchmark settings.

Time to first token, or TTFT, measures arrival to the first visible generated token. It includes waiting, prompt processing, sampling, and transport. For N greater than one, average time per output token, or TPOT, can be defined as the time between first and last tokens divided by N minus one. Individual inter-token gaps reveal stalls that this average hides. Specify whether timestamps are measured at the client or engine; buffered streaming can make their results disagree.

Track p95 queue latency separately from p95 TTFT and p95 TPOT. Quantiles do not add: the request at the queue-time percentile need not be the request at the prefill-time percentile. Report completed output tokens per second alongside accepted requests, rejections, and SLO-compliant requests per second, often called goodput. Otherwise a server can appear faster by rejecting difficult work or quietly excluding timed-out requests.
sections.formula: TTFT = t_first_visible − t_arrival; TPOT = (t_last_visible − t_first_visible)/(N − 1), N > 1; goodput = SLO-compliant completed requests / elapsed seconds

sections.title: 2. Rebuild the batch at iteration boundaries
paragraphs: A static batch retains a fixed membership until its slowest sequence finishes. Variable output lengths therefore create wasted opportunities. Continuous batching revisits membership between model iterations: finished sequences leave, eligible requests enter, and surviving sequences retain their own KV state. Orca established iteration-level scheduling as a practical serving mechanism. The scheduling boundary matters: adding a request does not mean interrupting an arbitrary GPU kernel halfway through its execution.

Imagine A needs two more decode steps and B needs twenty. A fixed batch may leave A's capacity unavailable while B continues. With continuous scheduling, C can use that capacity after A finishes, provided C's prefill and KV allocation fit. This thought experiment predicts a utilization benefit, not a universal speedup: C might be expensive, the batch might already saturate compute, or memory pressure might force preemption.

Keep request state explicit: waiting, partially prefilled, decoding, canceled, or complete. A scheduler transition must agree with memory ownership and the output stream. Priorities can select among eligible requests, but strict priority without aging can starve low-priority tenants. An interview answer should name the fairness rule, such as tenant quotas plus increasing priority with waiting age, and the consequence of reserving capacity for interactive traffic.

sections.title: 3. Bound interference between prefill and decode
paragraphs: Prefill processes many known prompt positions in parallel, while ordinary autoregressive decode advances each sequence one token at a time. Long prefills often use compute efficiently; small decode batches often spend much of their time moving weights and KV data. These are workload-dependent tendencies, not permanent hardware classifications. Putting a large prefill beside active streams can lengthen their next token gap even when total device utilization looks excellent.

Chunked prefill divides a prompt across iterations while preserving attention to earlier prompt tokens through accumulated KV state. Sarathi-Serve combines this with scheduling that keeps ongoing decodes progressing. Smaller chunks offer more frequent opportunities to serve decodes; excessively small chunks add scheduling and kernel overhead and can delay first-token delivery. Larger chunks improve prompt processing efficiency but consume more of the iteration's latency budget. [Sarathi-Serve](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi24/presentation/agrawal) explains this tradeoff.

A token budget limits newly processed positions per iteration, not the total cached history. For example, a budget of 1,024 positions with 64 ordinary decoding sequences leaves at most 960 positions for prefill. That arithmetic is a packing constraint, not a latency prediction: attending over longer histories can make the same count slower. Profile iteration duration by prompt chunk size, active sequences, and context lengths before mapping a latency target into a token limit.

sections.title: 4. Admission is a promise about future work
paragraphs: Admission has at least three constraints: sequence slots, compute work per iteration, and resident KV capacity. Passing one does not imply passing the others. Prompt tokens consume memory now; generated tokens grow that allocation later. Reserving every request's maximum output is conservative but wastes capacity when outputs are short. Statistical overbooking increases utilization but requires an explicit fallback when growth exceeds expectations, such as bounded preemption, recomputation, or rejecting further arrivals.

Bound the ingress queue in requests and estimated work. Ten short prompts and ten enormous prompts are different backlogs. Give overload responses a retry policy with jitter and a retry limit; immediate synchronized retries can amplify congestion. Propagate client cancellation through the router and scheduler, then stop future work and release unshared allocations after in-flight device access is safe. Closing an HTTP socket alone does not prove that GPU work stopped.

Deadlines allow the system to reject work that can no longer be useful. Before admitting a long prompt, ask whether estimated waiting plus service can meet its remaining budget. Keep estimates conservative and monitor their errors. For slow clients, bound outbound buffers and choose a documented policy: cancel, disconnect, or temporarily pause generation with a memory charge. Backpressure must reach the source of excess work instead of merely moving an unbounded queue to another process.

sections.title: 5. Work a queue and latency budget numerically
paragraphs: Consider an illustrative deterministic mixed scheduler with 32 active decode sequences. Assume every iteration takes 20 milliseconds and can process 512 prefill positions while advancing each decoder once. Ignore networking, arrivals after time zero, and memory pressure. Four prompts, each 2,048 tokens, arrive together. Process their prefill chunks first-come, first-served and assume the final prefill iteration produces the first output token. Each prompt needs four iterations, or 80 milliseconds, of this shared service.

Their queue waits before first execution are 0, 80, 160, and 240 milliseconds. Their TTFT values are 80, 160, 240, and 320 milliseconds. Existing streams retain a 20-millisecond gap under the assumptions. Using the nearest-rank convention, the p95 queue wait among these four observations is 240 milliseconds and p95 TTFT is 320 milliseconds. Four samples cannot establish a production tail guarantee; the calculation demonstrates accounting only.

The effective prompt service rate is 512/0.020 = 25,600 tokens per second, equivalent to 12.5 such prompts per second. At ten arrivals per second, average prompt demand consumes 80 percent of that assumed capacity. Bursts still cause waiting; an average utilization below one does not bound p95 latency. The 32 existing streams deliver 1,600 output tokens per second, excluding new streams. Adding their decodes could invalidate the fixed iteration-time assumption.

For a 250-millisecond TTFT target, this model permits at most 170 milliseconds of waiting before an 80-millisecond prompt service. The fourth arrival therefore cannot meet the target on this worker without changing the schedule or capacity. Route it elsewhere or reject it explicitly. Round-robin chunking would distribute first execution more fairly but could worsen the earliest completions; evaluate the metric users actually experience rather than optimizing the reported queue timer alone.
sections.formula: Prompt service = ceil(2,048/512) × 20 ms = 80 ms; prompt capacity = 25,600 tokens/s ÷ 2,048 tokens/request = 12.5 requests/s

sections.title: 6. Speculation changes the scheduling unit
paragraphs: Speculative decoding proposes several tokens with a cheaper draft process and verifies them with the target model. For stochastic sampling, simply accepting tokens that look plausible changes the distribution. Exact speculative sampling uses acceptance min(1, p(x)/q(x)) for a proposed token x, where p is the target distribution and q the draft distribution at the same prefix. On rejection, sample from the normalized positive part of p minus q and discard the remaining draft suffix. With correct implementation, this preserves the target sampling distribution, not necessarily an identical random-seed trajectory. [Leviathan and colleagues](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/leviathan23a.html) provide the construction.

Speedup depends on accepted progress relative to draft, verification, and orchestration costs. If a hypothetical round commits three tokens in 45 milliseconds while ordinary decoding costs 20 milliseconds per token, its local speedup is 60/45, or 1.33×. If it commits only one, it is slower. At high load, extra verification work and draft KV memory may reduce batch capacity. Measure accepted tokens per round and goodput under realistic concurrency before enabling speculation globally.
sections.formula: Illustrative speedup = committed tokens per round × baseline milliseconds per token / speculative milliseconds per round

sections.title: 7. Separate phases only when the transfer pays
paragraphs: Prefill/decode disaggregation assigns the phases to separate worker pools. DistServe shows how this permits different resource allocation and parallelism while removing direct interference on the same device. The price is moving or sharing KV state, maintaining compatible layouts, and scheduling across another queue. Bandwidth, topology, and prompt length affect whether the separation improves user-visible latency. [DistServe](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi24-zhong-yinmin.pdf) treats placement and communication as part of the design.

For a simple lower-bound calculation, transferring 2 GiB over an effective 25 GiB/s link costs 80 milliseconds before synchronization and queueing. That could erase a modest compute gain. Conversely, a high-bandwidth local link and strict streaming targets may justify separation. Reserve decode capacity before committing expensive prefill work; otherwise completed prompts can accumulate KV state while waiting downstream. Model transfer failures, cancellation during handoff, and ownership cleanup as ordinary states, not exceptional afterthoughts.

Defend the final choice with open-loop load tests that preserve the intended arrival rate even when the server slows. Sweep realistic prompt and output distributions, burstiness, chunk budgets, and concurrency. Record rejection fraction, cancellation cleanup delay, KV occupancy, preemptions, and client-visible latency percentiles. Compare colocated chunking against disaggregation at equal hardware cost and equal SLOs. All numbers in this article are analytical examples; no engine benchmark or deployment was executed.

interview.question: A chat service meets its median TTFT target, but p95 token gaps spike whenever document uploads arrive. GPU utilization is high. What would you change and how would you prove it helped?
interview.answer: First correlate long-prefill execution with the affected token gaps and separate engine time from client buffering. Use continuous batching with bounded prefill chunks, profile iteration duration, and reserve decode progress while applying aging so prompts cannot starve. Bound ingress by estimated work and KV headroom, propagate cancellations, and route or reject work that cannot meet its deadline. Replay an open-loop mixed workload and compare p95 TTFT, per-request TPOT, individual gaps, rejection rate, and goodput at equal hardware cost. If interference still prevents both SLOs, evaluate separate prefill/decode pools including transfer and downstream queue costs. A throughput gain alone is insufficient evidence.
followUps: How would output-length uncertainty change KV reservation?
Why can a lower p95 queue wait coexist with worse TTFT?
When could speculative decoding reduce server goodput?
How would tenant fairness interact with deadline scheduling?

pitfalls: Adding separate p95 component latencies as if they describe the same request.
Treating an iteration token limit as a KV-memory limit or a guaranteed duration.
Reporting output throughput without rejection, timeout, and cancellation denominators.
Allowing decode priority to starve new prompts indefinitely.
Assuming a disconnected client automatically releases engine state.
Claiming exact speculative sampling means identical outputs for every random seed.
Comparing disaggregated and colocated serving without equal hardware and transfer accounting.
checklist: Specify client-visible TTFT, TPOT, token-gap, and rejection targets by workload class.
Measure arrivals and prompt/output length distributions, including bursts and cancellations.
Profile mixed-iteration duration before setting chunk and token budgets.
Enforce sequence, compute, KV-growth, and bounded-queue constraints separately.
Test cancellation, deadline expiry, slow clients, and memory-pressure recovery.
Measure speculative acceptance and goodput at target concurrency.
Include KV transfer time and downstream reservations in disaggregation decisions.
Run open-loop load sweeps and compare goodput at equal cost and SLOs.

flashcards.back: Arrival-to-first-token time includes queueing, prompt execution, sampling, and transport or buffering, so faster kernels alone may not fix it.

flashcards.front: Why inspect inter-token gaps as well as average TPOT?
flashcards.back: TPOT averages the first-to-last interval over N−1 gaps. A long stall can disappear inside a good average while remaining obvious to a streaming user.

flashcards.front: Can p95 queue time and p95 prefill time be added to get p95 TTFT?
flashcards.back: Generally no: percentile components can come from different requests. Measure the end-to-end distribution directly.

flashcards.front: What is the scheduling boundary in continuous batching?
flashcards.back: Membership changes between iterations, allowing completed sequences to leave and eligible work to enter while survivors retain KV state.

flashcards.front: Why can high GPU utilization coexist with poor streaming latency?
flashcards.back: A large prefill can use the GPU efficiently while delaying the next decode step for many streams. Utilization measures busyness, not deadline satisfaction.

flashcards.front: What is the central chunked-prefill tradeoff?
flashcards.back: Smaller chunks create frequent decode opportunities but pay more overhead; larger chunks improve prefill efficiency while lengthening potential token gaps.

flashcards.front: Why are iteration token and KV budgets separate?
flashcards.back: The iteration budget counts new positions processed now, while KV memory holds historical positions across requests and grows during generation.

flashcards.front: Why not reserve every request's maximum possible output?
flashcards.back: It protects against growth but can waste capacity when actual outputs are short. Overbooking needs a deliberate recovery policy when predictions fail.
It must reach the scheduler, stop future device work, and release unshared state only after in-flight references are safe; disconnecting a socket is insufficient.

flashcards.front: With 512 prompt tokens per 20 ms iteration, how long does a 2,048-token prefill take?
flashcards.back: Four iterations, or 80 ms under the stated fixed-duration assumption. Queue and transport time must still be added to obtain TTFT.

flashcards.front: What preserves the target distribution in speculative sampling?
flashcards.back: Accept using min(1,p/q); on rejection sample from the normalized positive residual p−q. Plausibility checks alone would bias the output distribution.

flashcards.front: Why can speculation hurt at high concurrency?
flashcards.back: Draft execution, verification, and extra KV state consume resources. If accepted progress is insufficient or batch capacity falls, goodput can decline.

flashcards.front: What new bottleneck does prefill/decode separation introduce?
flashcards.back: KV handoff and another queue can dominate saved interference time, so bandwidth, placement, and decode reservations belong in the capacity model.

flashcards.front: Why use open-loop load generation to evaluate overload?
flashcards.back: It preserves offered arrivals when service slows, exposing queue growth. A client that waits before issuing each next request can hide the overload.
